data.title: Solid Earnings May Not Tell The Whole Story For Prakash Pipes (NSE:PPL)
data.description:
Prakash Pipes Limited's (NSE:PPL) healthy profit numbers didn't contain any surprises for investors. We think this is due to investors looking beyond the statutory profits and being concerned with what they see.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

A Closer Look At Prakash Pipes' Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. You could think of the accrual ratio from cashflow as the 'non-FCF profit ratio'.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

For the year to September 2026, Prakash Pipes had an accrual ratio of 0.26. Unfortunately, that means its free cash flow fell significantly short of its reported profits. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of ₹399m, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of ₹560.9m. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of ₹399m, this year, indicates high risk.

Note: we always recommend investors check balance sheet strength. Click here to be taken to our balance sheet analysis of Prakash Pipes.

Our Take On Prakash Pipes' Profit Performance

Prakash Pipes didn't convert much of its profit to free cash flow in the last year, which some investors may consider rather suboptimal. Therefore, it seems possible to us that Prakash Pipes' true underlying earnings power is actually less than its statutory profit. But at least holders can take some solace from the 5.8% EPS growth in the last year. Of course, we've only just scratched the surface when it comes to analysing its earnings; one could also consider margins, forecast growth, and return on investment, among other factors. With this in mind, we wouldn't consider investing in a stock unless we had a thorough understanding of the risks. data.title: What Analog Devices Bulls Got Right
data.description:
If you had read only Analog Devices’ earnings headlines this year, the scale of the shareholder payoff might still surprise you. For Analog Devices shareholders, the return over the past year was 69.7%, including dividends. That result landed after record Q3 2026 figures and a wave of AI focused acquisitions that arrived well after the original 2025 debates about robotics growth and geopolitical risk. If you were weighing ADI on 19 November 2025, which signals really justified taking that ride?

On Simply Wall St, a Narrative is an investor's thesis written down: the reasoning, plus the numbers it rests on. Run those numbers and you get an estimated Fair Value.

This theme extends beyond Analog Devices. See which of 53 AI infrastructure stocks may still merit a closer look.

The Argument You Would Have Been Weighing Up On Analog Devices

The shares cost US$232 at the start of the period, and investors were effectively choosing between two very different stories for Analog Devices.

The bullish narrative put fair value at US$267, based on assumptions that revenue could grow 11.3% a year with profit margins reaching 34.6% and a future P/E of 34.6x over roughly three years.

The bearish view pointed to fair value of US$155, highlighting risks that large automotive and electronics customers might increasingly build chips in-house, which could pressure demand and margins for Analog Devices.

What The Results Changed For The Analog Devices Debate

Analog Devices then reported Q3 2026 revenue of US$4.02b and net income of US$1.34b, with net margin at 33.3% compared with 18.0% in Q3 2025. That result leaned toward the bullish story that called for higher profitability, although sector selloffs during 2026 reminded investors that strong reports do not remove cyclical or competitive risk.

The key lesson is simple. When a thesis hinges on better margins, track net margin in the filings and see whether it is actually moving toward the scenario you are paying for.

What Analog Devices’ Current Price Already Bakes In

Analog Devices now trades at US$377, with this Narrative’s Fair Value sitting above that level according to the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St. The current debate is less about whether the business has multiple growth avenues and more about how fully the share price already reflects them.

The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St leans on AI data center spending, aerospace and defense programs and rising automotive content as the core drivers behind that higher figure. A buyer today needs to judge whether Analog Devices can keep converting those design wins into high margin revenue over several years.

"The main thing that has to go right is that Analog Devices converts its expanding AI, aerospace and defense, automotive and industrial design win pipeline into sustained high-margin revenue while managing input cost inflation and cybersecurity risk."

That disagreement has a full argument behind it. → Uncover the higher Fair Value this Narrative argues for

Where Analog Devices’ Demand Echoes

Analog Devices benefits as customers upgrade factories, vehicles and data centers for AI workloads.

Those customers increasingly want full AI systems, not just individual chips or boards.

They are investing in complete computing platforms that convert power and cooling into trained models.

Another specialist concentrates on building those integrated AI stacks with processors, networking and software.

As more budgets favor these ready made AI factories, that quiet provider becomes harder to ignore.
